title: GPU node kernel panic — field notes and triage checklist
content:
Purpose:
Quick field notes for on-call engineers encountering kernel panics on GPU nodes. This is intentionally shorthand — meant to be used while diagnosing, not the canonical postmortem.

Symptoms we've seen in the wild (common patterns):
- sudden kernel oops/panic during high-throughput inference jobs (usually long sequences or batch spikes)
- node becomes unresponsive to SSH; IPMI still reachable sometimes
- dmesg/journalctl shows GPU-related stack traces, e.g. printk backtraces referencing nvidia.ko or amdgpu depending on fleet
- ECC counts spike in monitoring before panic (single-bit or corrected errors)
- NVLink flaps logged as link reset, followed by driver reinitialization attempts
- kernel taint flags present after driver crash (proprietary module loaded)

Immediate triage checklist (what to run quickly while node is still accessible):
- Check node responsiveness: ping, ssh (if slow, prefer IPMI console).
- Run: sudo journalctl -k -b --no-pager | tail -n 200 (look for 'kernel panic', 'oops', 'nvidia', 'GPU', 'mm', 'nvlink')
- Check ECC/thermal metrics: sudo nvidia-smi -q -d ECC,THERMAL,POWER (or vendor tool for AMD)
- If SSH alive: sudo dmesg --color=never | tail -n 200
- Check for compactions or OOM killer events: sudo journalctl -u kubelet --since "-30m"
- Inspect NVLink and PCI errors: sudo journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'nvlink|pci|link'
- If driver appears crashed: lsmod | grep nvidia; sudo modinfo nvidia | head -n 5
- Capture kernel oops: sudo cat /proc/sys/kernel/printk and /proc/last_kmsg (if configured)
- If possible, enable kdump or copy vmcore once available: check /var/crash or configured dump path

Useful live commands (cheat sheet):
- nvidia-smi -q -g 0  # quick per-GPU health
- nvidia-smi --loop-ms=1000 -q  # watch for thermal/ECC spikes (limited use in prod)
- sudo perf top -g  # if kernel is responsive and you suspect CPU lockups
- sudo echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches  # quick memory sanity (note: intrusive)
- sudo cat /sys/kernel/debug/dri/0/i915_error_state  # example for Intel integrated (if applicable)

Crash evidence examples (real-ish excerpts for pattern matching):
- Example A (kernel oops referencing NV driver):
  "[ 1867.429851] NVRM: Xid (0001:04): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus.
  [ 1867.429860] nvidia 0000:04:00.0: GPU crash dump saved to /var/log/nvidia/gpu0/rx_12345.dmp
  [ 1867.430010] kernel: Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt"
- Example B (ECC counts then panic):
  "[ 512.231122] gpu0: ECC corrected count: 27
  [ 512.231128] gpu0: ECC corrected count: 28
  [ 512.241910] kernel: BUG: unable to handle kernel NULL pointer dereference at 0000000000000000"
- Example C (NVLink reset storms):
  "[ 1200.005] nvlink0: link down
  [ 1200.005] nvlink0: reinitializing link
  [ 1200.006] nvidia: failed to reinitialize NVLink, resetting driver"

Heuristics / quick root-cause filters (what to check first):
1) ECC spike present in the last 10 minutes? -> suspect hardware/thermal degradation or PCIe signal integrity. Move node to quarantine in scheduler, open hw ticket.
2) NVLink resets without ECC -> suspect firmware/driverncompatibility or cabling between GPUs (on DGX-like nodes). Check firmware mismatch matrix (vendor doc).
3) Immediate 'GPU fell off the bus' / Xid 79 -> usually driver/firmware/hardware. Collect dmesg, nv-dump, and escalate to hardware ops.
4) OOM or page faults in GPU user-space -> check model memory patterns and batch sizes; reproduce in canary nodes with same model.

Field-run runbook snippets (keep short, actionable):
- If node is unresponsive but IPMI reachable: capture BMC console logs, graceful powercycle via IPMI (soft-reset first), tag node as 'isolated' in inventory.
- If node reboots repeatedly on boot: attach kernel cmdline to serial console, enable kdump on next boot, do not re-image until hardware ops inspects PCIe seating and power cables.
- For NVLink-specific errors: check cabling/fabric (if custom build), vendor firmware version (nvlink fw), driver version. Coordinate with vendor rep before mass reboots.

Data to collect for any escalation (minimum):
- kernel logs (journalctl -k, dmesg) from 10m before to crash time
- nvidia-smi -q output and any dump files from /var/log/nvidia or /var/crash
- lspci -vvv output for GPU devices and PCI bridges
- kernel config (cat /proc/config.gz if present) and uname -a
- output of sensors / thermal drivers
- workload replication recipe (command line, image tag, model name, sequence length, batching parameters)

On-call heuristics (priority guidance):
- Severity P0: cluster-wide regression (>=5 nodes in 15m) or persistent SLO impact for critical customer routes. Escalate to on-call SRE lead + hardware ops immediately.
- Severity P1: single-node but production-impacting for dedicated customers. Isolate node, drain pods, and attach hardware ticket.
- P2/P3: single-job failures with low blast radius — schedule repro and diagnostic window.

Known mitigations (short-term):
- Auto-drain & isolate: our scheduler should taint node on >X ECC corrected errors within 1 hour. Confirm taint thresholds (ticketed: infra-123).
- Driver rollback: ephemeral rollback to last-known-good driver on a small subset of nodes for canary. Must coordinate with release-eng.
- Reduce batch sizes / limit max tokens for suspect workloads as temporary mitigation (via per-route throttles in Redwood Console).

Post-incident follow-ups to add to permanent runbook (todo):
- Standardize kdump + vmcore collection across GPU fleet (configure central crashstore).
- Add NVLink firmware matrix to internal runbook (mapping: node hw rev -> tested fw -> driver).
- Implement automated ECC anomaly detection (alert when corrected errors trend up per GPU).
- Create minimal reproducible test that stresses NVLink (scripts + canary nodes).
- Document safe driver rollback playbook with step-by-step rollback + verification tests.

Open questions / notes to self:
- Do we want an automated scheduler policy that retires nodes after N corrected ECCs in M days? (tradeoff: false positives vs safety)
- How often do kernel upgrades correlate with these driver panics? Need cross-correlation across kernel and driver rollouts.
- Can we add non-invasive NVLink health telemetry to Prometheus? Current vendor tools are pull-only and rate-limited.

Recent quick debugging timeline (real incident shorthand):
- 2025-06-08 03:12 UTC: Node ip-10-20-30-45 starts cycling; SLO alerts triggered for hosted-api/generate route.
- 03:13: SSH unresponsive; IPMI console shows kernel stacktrace.
- 03:14: oncall ran journalctl -k and saw "GPU has fallen off the bus" + Xid 79.
- 03:20: Node isolated, workload shifted. Hardware ops pulled logs, attached nv-dumps.
- 03:44: Vendor requested vmcore; kdump not configured -> delay.
- 06:10: Node rebooted with same driver; hardware ops replaced GPU board (suspected failing GPU).

Action items (assignments):
- (Aisha) draft vendor firmware compatibility matrix (due 2025-07-01).
- (Liam) instrument ECC anomaly alert (small PR to metrics pipeline, due 2025-06-27).
- (Priya) write kdump centralization runbook (due 2025-06-30).

Quick references (internal):
- Kernel oops decoding guide: https://confluence.redwood-inference.internal/kernel-oops-guide
- NV driver Xid reference (vendor): https://vendor.docs/nvidia/xid-codes
- Hardware ops contact in PagerDuty: HW-ONCALL (see infra docs)

If you're reading this on-call: breathe. Follow the checklist, isolate the node, gather evidence, and escalate early if you see ECC spikes or Xid 79. This doc is a living set of notes — push fixes/PRs to the runtime repo and link them above.
